title: Train, dev and test
objectives: Split names into train, dev and test sets, and say what each one is for.

screens.title: A loss on what?
screens.prose: A colleague says: “my name model’s loss is 2.14.” The table shows our MLP scored on three sets of names.

screens.question: Which of these is the MLP’s loss?

2.1356, the lowest of the three

options.text: 2.1742, the highest of the three

Each is the average loss on a different set of names.

feedback.correct: All three: the same model scores differently on different names.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask what each column measures.

byKey.train: You picked the friendliest number. On the names it trained on, a model always looks its best.

explain.text: One set of weights gives 2.1356 on the training names, 2.1609 on dev and 2.1742 on test. A loss is only meaningful with the names it was measured on.

explain.text: $\lfloor 0.8 \times 32{,}033 \rfloor = 25{,}626$ and $\lfloor 0.9 \times 32{,}033 \rfloor = 28{,}829$, so dev holds 3,203 names and test the last 3,204. Splitting by names keeps all of a name’s rows together.

screens.prose: You chose the MLP’s step size on dev, its size on dev, and the bigram’s $\alpha$ on dev. Now you write up the result.

The dev losses, since they chose the settings

options.text: The training losses, the most precise
options.why: Training losses measure fit, not how the model does on new names.

screens.title: Choosing on test
screens.prose: A learner tries 40 settings, scores each on the test names, keeps the best and reports its test loss of 2.13.

state.caption: Average loss in nats a letter on each set of names.

screens.question: What is wrong with the 2.13?

options.text: Test chose it: 2.13 is optimistic
Nothing: it is a test loss
options.why: It is measured on test, but test also picked it; the best of 40 noisy scores is biased low.

options.text: Only that 40 settings is too few
options.why: More settings would make it worse: more chances for a lucky score.

hints.text: The best of 40 scores on one set is the luckiest, not the truest.

feedback.correct: Test chose the model, so 2.13 is the best of 40 draws: biased low.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask what the test set was used for.

byKey.fine: You trusted the label “test”. Once the test names choose the model, the hold-out is no longer held out.

explain.text: Each test score is the true loss plus noise; picking the least of 40 picks the luckiest noise. The hold-out is no longer held out, so 2.13 overstates the model. Choose on dev and test once.

screens.title: Rows of one name
screens.prose: Splitting by rows puts emma’s five rows in different sets. Splitting by names avoids that, but the file repeats names: it has 32,033 lines and only 29,494 different names, so 390 of the 3,203 dev names also appear among the training names.

screens.question: What share of the dev names also appear in the training names? Give a decimal to 2 places.

feedback.correct: $390 / 3{,}203 = 0.12$: about one dev name in eight is a repeat of a training name.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide the repeats by the dev names.

byKey.distinct: That is the share of repeated lines in the whole file. The question asks about the dev names.

explain.text: 390 of the 3,203 dev names, 0.12, also occur in the training names, because popular names appear more than once in the file. That is part of the task, as new names will include common ones; splitting by rows would leak far more.

screens.title: Dev below train
screens.prose: The bigram scores 2.4536 on its training names and 2.4514 on dev: lower on names it never counted.

state.caption: Average loss in nats a letter on each set of names.

screens.question: How can the dev loss be below the training loss?

options.text: By chance, in a finite sample
It must be a bug: dev can never beat train
options.why: For a tiny model the train advantage is small, and a sample of 3,203 names can fall either side.

options.text: The dev names leaked into the counts
options.why: The counts come from the training names only; the dev names played no part.

hints.text: How big is the bigram’s advantage on its own names?
Tiny: it has only 729 numbers, so the sample noise of dev can outweigh it.

feedback.correct: Chance: with a small model, the gap is smaller than the noise of a finite dev set.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare the size of the effect with the noise.

byKey.bug: You treated “dev above train” as a law. It is a tendency, swamped here by sampling noise.

explain.text: A model fits its training names a little better than new ones, but the bigram has only 729 numbers, so that advantage is tiny. The dev set is a finite sample, and its loss landed 0.002 below; on test it is 2.4702, above.

screens.title: split_names() in code
screens.prose: Write `split_names(words, seed)`: shuffle the positions with `np.random.default_rng(seed).permutation(n)`, then cut at `int(0.8 * n)` and `int(0.9 * n)`. Return the lists `(train, dev, test)` in the shuffled order.
screens.question: Write `split_names`.

widget.solution:
import numpy as np


def split_names(words, seed):
    n = len(words)
    perm = np.random.default_rng(seed).permutation(n)
    n1, n2 = int(0.8 * n), int(0.9 * n)
    train = [words[i] for i in perm[:n1]]
    dev = [words[i] for i in perm[n1:n2]]
    test = [words[i] for i in perm[n2:]]
    return train, dev, test
widget.how: Submit runs 5 hidden tests: the sizes and the first three training names for seed 42, and that the three sets together are exactly the 32,033 names. Then come a planted list of ten and the first two dev names for seed 7. Each answer must equal the expected value exactly.

mutants.source:
import numpy as np


def split_names(words, seed):
    n = len(words)
    perm = np.random.default_rng(42).permutation(n)
    n1, n2 = int(0.8 * n), int(0.9 * n)
    train = [words[i] for i in perm[:n1]]
    dev = [words[i] for i in perm[n1:n2]]
    test = [words[i] for i in perm[n2:]]
    return train, dev, test

hints.text: Shuffle positions, not the names themselves.
`perm[:n1]`, `perm[n1:n2]` and `perm[n2:]`, each turned back into names.

feedback.correct: Your split matches the course: 25,626, 3,203 and 3,204, starting briah, xzayvion, amad.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Read the first failing test.

explain.text: One seeded permutation of positions, cut at $\lfloor 0.8n \rfloor$ and $\lfloor 0.9n \rfloor$, gives three disjoint sets that cover every line. NumPy’s generator makes the same permutation in the app as on a desktop.

screens.title: A live period
screens.prose: A fund develops strategies on 2010 to 2019 data, tunes them on 2020 to 2021, and plans to judge the winner on 2022 to 2024. After a poor result on 2022 to 2024, it tweaks the strategy and checks 2022 to 2024 again.
screens.question: What is left of the fund’s test period?

options.text: Nothing: it is no longer held out
All of it: the data has not changed
options.why: The data is the same, but it has been used to choose; any later score on it is optimistic.

options.text: Half of it, after one look
options.why: One look that changes the strategy is enough to spend it.

hints.text: Which job did 2022 to 2024 just do?
It chose a tweak: that is the dev job.

feedback.correct: It has become dev data; the fund needs fresh data, such as live trading, to test.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Ask what the period was used for.

byKey.ok: You trusted the dates. Once a period chooses the strategy, its score is no longer a test.

explain.text: Tweaking after seeing 2022 to 2024 turns it into tuning data, as testing level 3 warned. The only honest test left is data the fund has not seen, such as the next year of live trading.
